title: Math is Explaining and Sharing
contentObjective: I can construct an argument using equations, drawings, or words, and use volume to defend a recommendation.
languageObjective: I can explain my thinking with clear math vocabulary using the words argument, conjecture, and cubic units.

vocabulary.definition: A chain of reasons — equations, drawings, or words — used to defend your thinking.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una cadena de razones — ecuaciones, dibujos o palabras — que usas para defender tu pensamiento.
vocabulary.example: I recommend two jumbo boxes because their total volume is greater.
vocabulary.cloze: A chain of reasons used to defend your thinking is an ___.

examples.text: A claim followed by the computation that supports it
examples.why: The reasons are attached to the claim.
A claim with no reasons behind it convinces nobody.

vocabulary.definition: A mathematical statement you believe is true but have not yet proven.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una afirmación matemática que crees verdadera pero que aún no has probado.
vocabulary.example: I think the two jumbo boxes hold more cereal than the three large boxes.
vocabulary.visual: “A bigger box ALWAYS holds more cereal” — believed, not yet proven.
vocabulary.cloze: A statement you believe is true but have not yet proven is a ___.

examples.text: “I think the two jumbo boxes hold more cereal.”
examples.why: It is a checkable claim that still needs an argument.
That is a definition already established, not a claim to test.

vocabulary.definition: A single example that shows a statement is not always true.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un solo ejemplo que muestra que una afirmación no siempre es verdadera.
vocabulary.example: One box with more volume but more empty air space inside.
vocabulary.visual: One jumbo box sold half full of air breaks “bigger always holds more”.
vocabulary.cloze: A single case that shows a statement is not always true is a ___.

examples.text: A larger box holding less cereal than a smaller one
examples.why: One case is enough to make the ALWAYS claim false.

examples.text: Another box that fits the claim
examples.why: Agreeing examples never disprove a statement.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of space a solid figure takes up, measured in cubic units.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La cantidad de espacio que ocupa una figura sólida, medida en unidades cúbicas.
vocabulary.example: A garden bed 4 ft long, 3 ft wide, and 2 ft deep has a volume of 24 cubic feet.
vocabulary.visual: 8 in × 3 in × 10 in = 240 cubic inches of cereal space.
vocabulary.cloze: The amount of space a solid figure takes up, in cubic units, is its ___.

examples.text: How much soil fills a 4 ft × 2 ft × 1 ft planter
examples.why: It measures the space inside, in cubic units.

examples.text: How much wrapping paper covers the box
examples.why: That is surface area — the outside, not the inside.

vocabulary.definition: A cube with edges 1 unit long — the unit used to measure volume.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un cubo cuyas aristas miden 1 unidad — la unidad que se usa para medir el volumen.
vocabulary.example: The community garden needs 48 cubic feet of soil.
vocabulary.visual: One cube, 1 unit on every edge — the block volume is counted in.
vocabulary.cloze: A cube with edges 1 unit long, used to measure volume, is a ___ ___.

examples.why: A cube 1 foot on each edge.
A square unit covers flat space; it has no depth.

launch.narrative: Yuzuki is buying her favorite breakfast cereal. She can buy three large-sized boxes or two jumbo-sized boxes for the same price. Which option should she pick — and can you convince a classmate you are right?

conceptIntro.heading: When we do math, we develop arguments to defend our thinking
conceptIntro.intro: Getting an answer is only half the work. The other half is explaining it so clearly — with conjectures, examples, and counterexamples — that someone else can decide whether your argument is convincing.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Math Practices: Mathematical Arguments & Justification. 1. State a clear claim or conjecture supported by calculations. 2. Use accurate units and vocabulary (e.g. cubic units for volume). 3. Test with counterexamples to verify that the rule holds true every time

iDo.title: Watch me argue with equations
lines: Suppose each large box is 8 inches long, 3 inches wide, and 10 inches tall. Its volume is 8 × 3 × 10 = 240 cubic inches, so three large boxes hold 240 × 3 = 720 cubic inches.
Suppose each jumbo box is 10 inches long, 4 inches wide, and 10 inches tall. Its volume is 10 × 4 × 10 = 400 cubic inches, so two jumbo boxes hold 400 × 2 = 800 cubic inches.
I recommend buying two jumbo boxes because 800 cubic inches is greater than 720 cubic inches — the total volume is greater, so there is more cereal for the same price.
linesEs: Supongamos que cada caja grande mide 8 pulgadas de largo, 3 de ancho y 10 de alto. Su volumen es 8 × 3 × 10 = 240 pulgadas cúbicas, así que tres cajas grandes contienen 240 × 3 = 720 pulgadas cúbicas.
Supongamos que cada caja jumbo mide 10 pulgadas de largo, 4 de ancho y 10 de alto. Su volumen es 10 × 4 × 10 = 400 pulgadas cúbicas, así que dos cajas jumbo contienen 400 × 2 = 800 pulgadas cúbicas.
Recomiendo comprar dos cajas jumbo porque 800 pulgadas cúbicas es más que 720 pulgadas cúbicas — el volumen total es mayor, así que hay más cereal por el mismo precio.

weDo.title: Let's argue with words together
lines: Not every good reason is an equation. Finish this argument: “I recommend buying two jumbo boxes because …”
The book offers two word-based reasons: there is less packaging with two boxes, and two boxes are easier to store than three boxes.

Now listen to the other side. One student recommends the three large boxes because the cereal will stay fresher — each box is open for less time — and because greater volume does not always mean more cereal inside.
How convincing is each argument? That judgment is math too.
linesEs: No toda buena razón es una ecuación. Termina este argumento: «Recomiendo comprar dos cajas jumbo porque…»
El libro ofrece dos razones con palabras: hay menos empaque con dos cajas, y dos cajas son más fáciles de guardar que tres.

Ahora escucha el otro lado. Un estudiante recomienda las tres cajas grandes porque el cereal se mantendrá más fresco — cada caja está abierta menos tiempo — y porque más volumen no siempre significa más cereal adentro.
¿Qué tan convincente es cada argumento? Ese juicio también es matemática.

youDo.title: Now you try
lines: Write one more argument for the three large boxes, and one more for the two jumbo boxes.
Then trade with a partner and say which of their arguments you find most convincing, and why.
linesEs: Escribe un argumento más a favor de las tres cajas grandes y uno más a favor de las dos cajas jumbo.
Luego intercambia con un compañero y di cuál de sus argumentos te parece más convincente, y por qué.

interactiveVisual.label: The cereal box: 8 in by 3 in by 10 in.

conceptIntro.headingEs: Cuando hacemos matemáticas, armamos argumentos para defender nuestro razonamiento
conceptIntro.introEs: Obtener una respuesta es solo la mitad del trabajo. La otra mitad es explicarla con tanta claridad — con conjeturas, ejemplos y contraejemplos — que otra persona pueda decidir si tu argumento la convence.
conceptIntro.keyIdeaEs: Prácticas matemáticas: argumentos matemáticos y justificación. 1. Enuncia una afirmación o conjetura clara respaldada por cálculos. 2. Usa unidades y vocabulario precisos (por ejemplo, unidades cúbicas para el volumen). 3. Ponla a prueba con contraejemplos para verificar que la regla se cumpla siempre

discourse.sentenceFrameEs: Un argumento con ___ es más fuerte aquí porque ___.

connect.scenario: A neighborhood group is building a community garden. To fill the beds they need soil — and to order the right amount, they need volume, measured precisely in cubic units. One design needs 48 cubic feet of soil.
connect.promptQuestion: How can the group determine the amount of soil needed, and how can they check that their answer is accurate?
connect.prompt: To find how much soil is needed, find the ___ of the garden beds. Because volume covers three dimensions, label the answer in ___ feet. Finding the volume two different ways and getting matching totals shows the solution is ___.

check.stem: The group needs to order soil to fill the garden beds. Which unit should they use to express the amount of soil?
check.explanation: Cubic feet correctly matches the beds' real-world scale. Feet only measures length (one dimension); square feet measures area (two dimensions, like a floor); cubic inches uses the right idea but too small a unit for garden-bed dimensions given in feet.
check.stemEs: El grupo necesita pedir tierra para llenar las jardineras. ¿Qué unidad deben usar para expresar la cantidad de tierra?
check.explanationEs: Los pies cúbicos corresponden correctamente a la escala real de las jardineras. Los pies solo miden longitud (una dimensión); los pies cuadrados miden área (dos dimensiones, como un piso); las pulgadas cúbicas usan la idea correcta pero una unidad demasiado pequeña para dimensiones de jardinera dadas en pies.
choicesEs: pies
pies cuadrados
pies cúbicos
pulgadas cúbicas
choiceFeedback: Length alone only measures one direction — soil needs a unit that captures space in three directions.
An area unit measures a flat surface — soil needs a unit that also accounts for depth.
That unit has the right idea but is far too small for beds measured in feet.
choiceFeedbackEs: La longitud sola mide solo una dirección — el suelo necesita una unidad que capture espacio en tres direcciones.
Una unidad de área mide una superficie plana — el suelo también necesita contar la profundidad.
Esa unidad tiene la idea correcta pero es demasiado pequeña para camas medidas en pies.

check.stem: After finding the volume of the garden beds one way, what should the group do to be confident their total of 48 cubic feet is accurate?
choices: Round the answer to the nearest ten
Decompose the figure a second, different way and check that both totals match
Multiply the total by 2 just to be safe
Ask a classmate if the number sounds right
check.explanation: Recomputing volume with an independent method and getting the same total is what actually confirms accuracy. Rounding changes the answer instead of checking it, multiplying by 2 has no mathematical reason behind it, and asking if a number 'sounds right' isn't a calculation check.
check.stemEs: Después de hallar el volumen de las jardineras de una manera, ¿qué debe hacer el grupo para estar seguro de que su total de 48 pies cúbicos es exacto?
check.explanationEs: Volver a calcular el volumen con un método independiente y obtener el mismo total es lo que de verdad confirma la exactitud. Redondear cambia la respuesta en vez de comprobarla, multiplicar por 2 no tiene ninguna razón matemática detrás, y preguntar si un número «suena bien» no es una comprobación de cálculo.
choicesEs: Redondear la respuesta a la decena más cercana
Descomponer la figura de una segunda manera distinta y revisar que los dos totales coincidan
Multiplicar el total por 2 nada más por si acaso
Preguntarle a un compañero si el número suena bien
choiceFeedback: Rounding changes your number — it doesn't confirm whether the original calculation was correct.
There's no mathematical reason to double the total — that doesn't check the first calculation.
A gut check from someone else isn't the same as recomputing the volume to confirm it.
choiceFeedbackEs: Redondear cambia tu número — no confirma si el cálculo original estuvo correcto.
No hay una razón matemática para duplicar el total — eso no comprueba el primer cálculo.
Que alguien diga si suena bien no es lo mismo que volver a calcular el volumen para confirmarlo.

check.stem: The group decides to decompose the garden bed design into simpler shapes to find its volume. What does that method involve?
choices: Breaking the figure into rectangular prisms, finding each prism's volume, then adding them
Adding the areas of each face of the figure
Multiplying the total length by the total width only
Averaging the volumes of similar containers they've seen before
check.explanation: Decomposing means splitting the irregular figure into rectangular prisms, finding length x width x height for each piece, then summing those volumes. Adding face areas finds surface area, not volume; multiplying only length by width leaves out height; averaging unrelated containers ignores the actual dimensions.
check.stemEs: El grupo decide descomponer el diseño de la jardinera en figuras más simples para hallar su volumen. ¿Qué implica ese método?
check.explanationEs: Descomponer significa separar la figura irregular en prismas rectangulares, hallar largo x ancho x altura de cada pieza y luego sumar esos volúmenes. Sumar áreas de caras halla el área de la superficie, no el volumen; multiplicar solo largo por ancho deja fuera la altura; promediar recipientes que no tienen relación ignora las dimensiones reales.
choicesEs: Separar la figura en prismas rectangulares, hallar el volumen de cada prisma y luego sumarlos
Sumar las áreas de cada cara de la figura
Multiplicar solo el largo total por el ancho total
Promediar los volúmenes de recipientes parecidos que hayan visto antes
choiceFeedback: Adding up the face areas gives surface area, not the volume inside the figure.
Multiplying only length by width leaves out height, so it can't give a volume.
Guessing from other containers ignores this figure's actual measurements.
choiceFeedbackEs: Sumar las áreas de las caras da el área de superficie, no el volumen dentro de la figura.
Multiplicar solo el largo por el ancho deja fuera la altura, así que no puede dar un volumen.
Adivinar a partir de otros recipientes ignora las medidas reales de esta figura.

connect.modelAnswer: I would decompose the garden beds into rectangular prisms and find each volume with length × width × height, then add them. Volume is measured in cubic units, so my answer is in cubic feet: 48 cubic feet of soil. To check accuracy I would decompose the figure a second, different way — if both ways give 48 cubic feet, the solutions match and the answer is accurate.
connect.promptEs: Para hallar cuánta tierra se necesita, halla el ___ de las jardineras. Como el volumen cubre tres dimensiones, escribe la respuesta en pies ___. Hallar el volumen de dos maneras distintas y obtener totales iguales muestra que la solución es ___.
connect.scenarioEs: Un grupo del vecindario está construyendo un jardín comunitario. Para llenar las jardineras necesitan tierra — y para pedir la cantidad correcta, necesitan el volumen, medido con precisión en unidades cúbicas. Un diseño necesita 48 pies cúbicos de tierra.
connect.promptQuestionEs: ¿Cómo puede el grupo determinar la cantidad de tierra necesaria, y cómo pueden comprobar que su respuesta es exacta?
connect.modelAnswerEs: Yo descompondría las jardineras en prismas rectangulares y hallaría cada volumen con largo × ancho × altura, y luego los sumaría. El volumen se mide en unidades cúbicas, así que mi respuesta va en pies cúbicos: 48 pies cúbicos de tierra. Para comprobar que es exacta, descompondría la figura de una segunda manera distinta — si las dos maneras dan 48 pies cúbicos, las soluciones coinciden y la respuesta es exacta.

approaching.stem: An egg muffin is about 60 calories. A plate holds 4 egg muffins. About how many calories are on the plate?
approaching.explanation: 4 muffins at about 60 calories each is 60 × 4 = 240 calories.
choiceFeedback: That divides 60 by 4 instead of multiplying.
That adds 60 + 4 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies 60 by 10 instead of by 4.
hints: How many muffins, and how many calories in each one?
4 equal groups of 60.
Multiply 60 × 4.
approaching.stemEs: Un panecillo de huevo tiene unas 60 calorías. Un plato lleva 4 panecillos de huevo. ¿Aproximadamente cuántas calorías hay en el plato?
approaching.explanationEs: 4 panecillos de unas 60 calorías cada uno es 60 × 4 = 240 calorías.
hintsEs: ¿Cuántos panecillos, y cuántas calorías tiene cada uno?
4 grupos iguales de 60.
Multiplica 60 × 4.

approaching.stem: A large cereal box is 8 in long, 3 in wide, and 10 in tall. What is its volume?
approaching.explanation: Volume of a rectangular prism is length × width × height: 8 × 3 × 10 = 240 cubic inches.
choiceFeedback: That adds 8 + 3 + 10 instead of multiplying the dimensions.
That multiplies only 8 × 10 and leaves out the 3-inch width.
The number is right, but volume is measured in CUBIC inches — square inches measure area.
hints: Volume of a box is length × width × height.
Multiply 8 × 3 first, then use the height.
approaching.stemEs: Una caja grande de cereal mide 8 pulgadas de largo, 3 de ancho y 10 de alto. ¿Cuál es su volumen?
approaching.explanationEs: El volumen de un prisma rectangular es largo × ancho × alto: 8 × 3 × 10 = 240 pulgadas cúbicas.
hintsEs: El volumen de una caja es largo × ancho × alto.
Multiplica primero 8 × 3 y luego usa la altura.

approaching.stem: Each jumbo box holds 400 cubic inches. How much do TWO jumbo boxes hold?
approaching.explanation: Two boxes of 400 cubic inches each is 400 × 2 = 800 cubic inches.
choiceFeedback: That divides 400 by 2 instead of doubling.
That adds 400 + 2 instead of doubling.
That multiplies 400 by 10 instead of by 2.
hints: Two equal boxes — what operation combines them?
Double 400.
approaching.stemEs: Cada caja jumbo contiene 400 pulgadas cúbicas. ¿Cuánto contienen DOS cajas jumbo?
approaching.explanationEs: Dos cajas de 400 pulgadas cúbicas cada una son 400 × 2 = 800 pulgadas cúbicas.
hintsEs: Dos cajas iguales — ¿qué operación las combina?
Duplica 400.

approaching.stem: Yuzuki can buy three large boxes or two jumbo boxes for the same price. Give ONE reason in words (no equations) for either choice.
approaching.modelAnswer: I recommend two jumbo boxes because there is less packaging, and two boxes are easier to store than three.
sentenceStems: A reason that is not about volume is ___ .
approaching.stemEs: Yuzuki puede comprar tres cajas grandes o dos cajas jumbo por el mismo precio. Da UNA razón en palabras (sin ecuaciones) a favor de cualquiera de las dos opciones.

approaching.stem: Which unit should the garden group use when reporting how much soil fills the beds?
approaching.explanation: Volume is measured in cubic units, so soil that fills a space is measured in cubic feet.
choiceFeedback: Feet measure length — one dimension, not the space inside the bed.
Square feet measure area — the flat top of the bed, not how deep the soil goes.
Degrees measure angles or temperature, not the space soil fills.
hints: Soil fills SPACE, not a line or a flat surface.
Which unit is for volume?
Volume is measured in cubic units.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál unidad debe usar el grupo del jardín al informar cuánta tierra llena los canteros?
approaching.explanationEs: El volumen se mide en unidades cúbicas, así que la tierra que llena un espacio se mide en pies cúbicos.
hintsEs: La tierra llena un ESPACIO, no una línea ni una superficie plana.
¿Cuál unidad es de volumen?
El volumen se mide en unidades cúbicas.

approaching.stem: Why does it help to explain your thinking to others instead of just giving the answer?
approaching.modelAnswer: When I explain my thinking, classmates can decide whether my argument is convincing, catch mistakes I missed, and connect my ideas to their own.
sentenceStems: When someone hears my reasons, they can ___ .
approaching.stemEs: ¿Por qué ayuda explicar tu razonamiento a los demás en vez de solo dar la respuesta?

approaching.instructions: Sort each question: does it ask about covering a surface (area) or filling a space (volume)?
approaching.instructionsEs: Clasifica cada pregunta: ¿trata de cubrir una superficie (área) o de llenar un espacio (volumen)?
approaching.label: Sort each question: area or volume?

categories.label: Volume — cubic units
items: How much soil fills the garden bed?
How much cereal fits inside the box?
How much water fills the fish tank?
itemsEs: ¿Cuánta tierra llena el cantero del jardín?
¿Cuánto cereal cabe dentro de la caja?

categories.label: Area — square units
items: How much paper covers the lid of the box?
How much paint covers one wall?
How much mulch covers the top of the bed?
itemsEs: ¿Cuánto papel cubre la tapa de la caja?
¿Cuánto mantillo cubre la parte de arriba del cantero?

hints: 'Fill' means the inside of a 3-D shape — that is volume, in cubic units.
'Cover' means a flat surface — that is area, in square units.
hintsEs: 'Llenar' se refiere al interior de una figura 3D: eso es volumen, en unidades cúbicas.
'Cubrir' se refiere a una superficie plana: eso es área, en unidades cuadradas.
approaching.explanation: Filling questions need all three dimensions — soil, cereal, and water occupy length × width × height, measured in cubic units. Covering questions are flat — a lid, a wall, and the top of a bed have only length × width, measured in square units. Confusing the two is exactly the '240 square inches' mistake this lesson corrects.
approaching.explanationEs: Las preguntas de llenar necesitan las tres dimensiones: la tierra, el cereal y el agua ocupan largo × ancho × alto, en unidades cúbicas. Las de cubrir son planas: una tapa, una pared y la parte de arriba de un cantero solo tienen largo × ancho, en unidades cuadradas. Confundirlas es exactamente el error de las '240 pulgadas cuadradas' que esta lección corrige.

onLevel.stem: Three large boxes hold 240 cubic inches each. Two jumbo boxes hold 400 cubic inches each. Which is the correct volume comparison?
choices: 240 cubic inches vs. 400 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
480 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
720 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
720 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the large option holds more
onLevel.explanation: 240 × 3 = 720 and 400 × 2 = 800; since 800 > 720, the two jumbo boxes hold more in total.
choiceFeedback: That compares one box of each size instead of the full purchase — three larges vs. two jumbos.
480 comes from 240 × 2 — the large option has THREE boxes, not two.
The totals are right, but 800 is GREATER than 720, so the jumbo option wins the comparison.
hints: Find each TOTAL before comparing.
Which total is greater?
onLevel.stemEs: Tres cajas grandes contienen 240 pulgadas cúbicas cada una. Dos cajas jumbo contienen 400 pulgadas cúbicas cada una. ¿Cuál es la comparación correcta de volumen?
onLevel.explanationEs: 240 × 3 = 720 y 400 × 2 = 800; como 800 > 720, las dos cajas jumbo contienen más en total.
hintsEs: Halla cada TOTAL antes de comparar.
¿Cuál total es mayor?

onLevel.stem: One garden bed is 4 ft long, 3 ft wide, and 2 ft deep. A second bed is 6 ft long, 2 ft wide, and 2 ft deep. How much soil fills BOTH beds?
onLevel.explanation: First bed: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cubic feet. Second bed: 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 cubic feet. Together: 24 + 24 = 48 cubic feet.
choiceFeedback: That adds all the dimensions (4+3+2+6+2+2) instead of multiplying within each bed.
24 cubic feet is only ONE bed — the problem asks for both.
That multiplies the two bed volumes (24 × ... ) too far — you ADD the volumes of the parts, you don't double the total.
hints: Find each bed's volume separately, then combine.
Add the two volumes.
onLevel.stemEs: Un cantero mide 4 pies de largo, 3 de ancho y 2 de profundidad. Un segundo cantero mide 6 pies de largo, 2 de ancho y 2 de profundidad. ¿Cuánta tierra llena AMBOS canteros?
onLevel.explanationEs: Primer cantero: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 pies cúbicos. Segundo cantero: 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 pies cúbicos. Juntos: 24 + 24 = 48 pies cúbicos.
hintsEs: Halla el volumen de cada cantero por separado y luego combínalos.
Suma los dos volúmenes.

onLevel.stem: The group found the volume by decomposing the garden into prisms and adding. Why would they compute it a SECOND, different way?
choices: Because the first way is always wrong
To get a bigger number for the soil order
If both ways give the same answer, the solution is accurate
Because volume changes each time you measure it
onLevel.explanation: The book models exactly this: two different decompositions both gave 48 cubic feet, so the solutions match and the answer is accurate.
choiceFeedback: The first way can be perfectly correct — the second way CONFIRMS it rather than replaces it.
Checking is about accuracy, not inflating the answer — both ways should give the SAME number.
The garden's volume is fixed — what could vary is our calculation, which is why we check it.
hints: What did the two solutions in the lesson have in common?
The solutions were the same for both ways.
Matching answers mean the calculation is accurate.
onLevel.stemEs: El grupo halló el volumen descomponiendo el jardín en prismas y sumando. ¿Por qué lo calcularían una SEGUNDA vez de otra manera?
onLevel.explanationEs: El libro modela exactamente esto: dos descomposiciones distintas dieron 48 pies cúbicos, así que las soluciones coinciden y la respuesta es correcta.
hintsEs: ¿Qué tenían en común las dos soluciones de la lección?
Las soluciones fueron las mismas por los dos caminos.
Respuestas que coinciden significan que el cálculo es correcto.

onLevel.stem: A student recommends the three large boxes because the cereal stays fresher — each box is open for less time. Is this argument convincing? Explain.
onLevel.modelAnswer: It is somewhat convincing because it uses a real reason that matters to Yuzuki, not just volume. But it would be stronger with evidence — like how long a box stays fresh once opened. An argument can be convincing without equations if the reasoning is clear.
onLevel.stemEs: Un estudiante recomienda las tres cajas grandes porque el cereal se mantiene más fresco — cada caja está abierta menos tiempo. ¿Es convincente ese argumento? Explica.

choices: “I think the two jumbo boxes hold more cereal than the three large boxes.”
onLevel.explanation: A conjecture is a mathematical claim you believe but have not yet proven — the jumbo-box claim needs an argument to back it up.
choiceFeedback: That is a computed fact, already verified — nothing left to prove.
That is a definition, true by agreement rather than something to test.
That is a plain event from the story, not a mathematical claim to defend.
hints: A conjecture still needs proving.
Which statement says 'I think' about something checkable?
Which one would you build an argument FOR?
onLevel.explanationEs: Una conjetura es una afirmación matemática que crees pero que aún no has demostrado — la afirmación de la caja jumbo necesita un argumento que la respalde.
hintsEs: Una conjetura todavía necesita demostrarse.
¿Cuál enunciado dice 'creo que' sobre algo que se puede comprobar?
¿A favor de cuál construirías un argumento?

onLevel.stem: Use precise vocabulary to explain how you would find the soil needed for a bed 5 ft long, 2 ft wide, and 2 ft deep. Include the answer with its unit.
onLevel.modelAnswer: I would find the volume of the rectangular prism by multiplying length × width × height: 5 × 2 × 2 = 20. Volume is measured in cubic units, so the bed needs 20 cubic feet of soil.
sentenceStems: I would find the ___ by multiplying ___ .
onLevel.stemEs: Usa vocabulario preciso para explicar cómo hallarías la tierra necesaria para un cantero de 5 pies de largo, 2 de ancho y 2 de profundidad. Incluye la respuesta con su unidad.

onLevel.label: Compute the volume of each cereal box.
onLevel.labelEs: Calcula el volumen de cada caja de cereal.
hints: Multiply two dimensions first, then multiply the result by the third.
Pick the friendliest pair first: 8 × 10 = 80, then × 5 — order doesn't change the volume.
hintsEs: Multiplica dos dimensiones primero y luego multiplica el resultado por la tercera.
Elige primero el par más amigable: 8 × 10 = 80, luego × 5; el orden no cambia el volumen.
onLevel.explanation: Volume multiplies all three dimensions: 8 × 3 × 10 = 240, 5 × 8 × 10 = 400, and 6 × 4 × 5 = 120 cubic inches. These are the large and jumbo boxes from the recommendation argument — the units are cubic because the cereal fills space.
onLevel.explanationEs: El volumen multiplica las tres dimensiones: 8 × 3 × 10 = 240, 5 × 8 × 10 = 400 y 6 × 4 × 5 = 120 pulgadas cúbicas. Son las cajas grande y gigante del argumento de recomendación; las unidades son cúbicas porque el cereal llena un espacio.

extending.stem: A student claims: “Greater box volume ALWAYS means more cereal inside.” Which is the best counterexample?
choices: A large box that costs more than a jumbo box
A jumbo box with more volume that is sold half-filled with air
Two jumbo boxes that are easier to store than three large boxes
A box of a different cereal brand
extending.explanation: A counterexample must break the claim itself: a bigger box holding less cereal (more air) shows greater volume does not guarantee more cereal.
choiceFeedback: Price does not test the claim — the claim links volume to AMOUNT of cereal, not cost.
Storage convenience is a different argument entirely; it says nothing about how much cereal is inside.
Changing the brand changes the product, but does not show a bigger box holding less cereal.
hints: A counterexample must make the claim FALSE in one case.
The claim connects volume to amount of cereal.
Find the case where volume is bigger but cereal is not.
extending.stemEs: Un estudiante afirma: “Más volumen de caja SIEMPRE significa más cereal adentro.” ¿Cuál es el mejor contraejemplo?
extending.explanationEs: Un contraejemplo debe romper la afirmación misma: una caja más grande que contiene menos cereal (más aire) muestra que más volumen no garantiza más cereal.
hintsEs: Un contraejemplo debe hacer FALSA la afirmación en un caso.
La afirmación conecta el volumen con la cantidad de cereal.
Halla el caso donde el volumen es mayor pero el cereal no.

extending.stem: The garden needs 48 cubic feet of soil. One decomposition used two prisms of 24 cubic feet each. Which of these is ANOTHER decomposition of the same garden volume?
extending.explanation: 4 × 4 × 2 = 32 and 4 × 2 × 2 = 16, and 32 + 16 = 48 cubic feet — the same total by a different split.
choiceFeedback: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 and 3 × 3 × 2 = 18 give 45 cubic feet, not 48.
4 × 4 × 2 = 32 twice gives 64 cubic feet, not 48.
6 × 4 × 2 = 48 and 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 give 56 cubic feet, not 48.
hints: Compute each prism's volume, then add.
The parts must total exactly 48.
extending.stemEs: El jardín necesita 48 pies cúbicos de tierra. Una descomposición usó dos prismas de 24 pies cúbicos cada uno. ¿Cuál de estas es OTRA descomposición del mismo volumen del jardín?
extending.explanationEs: 4 × 4 × 2 = 32 y 4 × 2 × 2 = 16, y 32 + 16 = 48 pies cúbicos — el mismo total con una división distinta.
hintsEs: Calcula el volumen de cada prisma y luego suma.
Las partes deben sumar exactamente 48.

extending.stem: Another garden bed design is also being considered. What information would you need to compare the two designs, and how would you argue for the one you recommend?
extending.modelAnswer: I would need the dimensions of each design so I could compute both volumes in cubic feet. Then I would build my argument with equations — the volumes — and with words, like which design fits the space better or is easier to reach. I would state my recommendation and defend it with both kinds of evidence.
extending.stemEs: También se está considerando otro diseño de cantero. ¿Qué información necesitarías para comparar los dos diseños, y cómo defenderías el que recomiendas?

extending.stem: Write TWO arguments for the same recommendation about Yuzuki's cereal — one using equations, one using only words. Then say which you think would convince a classmate more, and why.
extending.modelAnswer: Equation argument: 400 × 2 = 800 cubic inches and 240 × 3 = 720 cubic inches, and 800 > 720, so the two jumbo boxes hold more. Word argument: two boxes make less packaging waste and are easier to store. I think the equation argument convinces more people because the numbers can be checked, but the word argument matters to anyone with a small pantry.
sentenceStems: With words: ___ . The more convincing one is ___ because ___ .
extending.stemEs: Escribe DOS argumentos para la misma recomendación sobre el cereal de Yuzuki — uno usando ecuaciones y otro usando solo palabras. Luego di cuál crees que convencería más a un compañero, y por qué.

extending.label: Match each prism to a DIFFERENT prism with the SAME volume.
extending.labelEs: Empareja cada prisma con un prisma DIFERENTE que tenga el MISMO volumen.
hints: Compute each volume first — equal products are the matches.
Different shapes can hold exactly the same amount: that is the counterexample idea from this lesson.
hintsEs: Calcula cada volumen primero: los productos iguales son las parejas.
Figuras diferentes pueden contener exactamente lo mismo: esa es la idea del contraejemplo de esta lección.
extending.explanation: 8 × 3 × 10 and 6 × 4 × 10 both equal 240; 4 × 3 × 2 and 6 × 2 × 2 both equal 24; 5 × 8 × 10 and 20 × 10 × 2 both equal 400; 6 × 2 × 4 and 8 × 3 × 2 both equal 48. Two boxes with different shapes can hold the same amount — a taller box does not always mean more cereal, which is the counterexample that tests the claim in this lesson.
extending.explanationEs: 8 × 3 × 10 y 6 × 4 × 10 dan 240; 4 × 3 × 2 y 6 × 2 × 2 dan 24; 5 × 8 × 10 y 20 × 10 × 2 dan 400; 6 × 2 × 4 y 8 × 3 × 2 dan 48. Dos cajas con formas distintas pueden contener lo mismo: una caja más alta no siempre significa más cereal, que es el contraejemplo que pone a prueba la afirmación de esta lección.

practice.commonMistake: Reporting volume without cubic units — saying the garden needs '48 feet' of soil, which is a length, or '48 square feet', which is an area.

diagram.title: Which Option Holds More? (cubic inches)
diagram.caption: Three large boxes hold 240 x 3 = 720 cubic inches; two jumbo boxes hold 400 x 2 = 800. The taller bar is the evidence an equation argument would point at.

exitTicket.stem: Which statement best captures what this lesson means by 'Math is Explaining and Sharing'?
choices: We keep our methods private so nobody can copy our answers
An argument only counts in math if it uses equations
We communicate our reasoning, listen to classmates' arguments, decide whether they are convincing, and check our calculations for accuracy
Once you have an answer, checking it a second way is a waste of time
exitTicket.explanation: The summary says it directly: we communicate our reasoning, make conjectures, listen and probe classmates' arguments, communicate precisely, label units accurately, and check that our calculations are accurate.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It covers communicating, listening, precision, and checking.
Which option keeps all of those?
exitTicket.stemEs: ¿Qué afirmación capta mejor lo que esta lección quiere decir con «las matemáticas son explicar y compartir»?
choicesEs: Guardamos nuestros métodos en secreto para que nadie copie nuestras respuestas
Un argumento solo cuenta en matemáticas si usa ecuaciones
Comunicamos nuestro razonamiento, escuchamos los argumentos de nuestros compañeros, decidimos si son convincentes y comprobamos que nuestros cálculos sean exactos
Una vez que tienes una respuesta, comprobarla de otra manera es perder el tiempo
exitTicket.explanationEs: El resumen lo dice directamente: comunicamos nuestro razonamiento, hacemos conjeturas, escuchamos y cuestionamos los argumentos de nuestros compañeros, comunicamos con precisión, rotulamos las unidades con exactitud y comprobamos que nuestros cálculos sean exactos.
hintsEs: Vuelve a mirar la diapositiva de resumen.
Cubre comunicar, escuchar, la precisión y comprobar.
¿Qué opción conserva todas esas?
choiceFeedback: The lesson is about sharing and explaining your reasoning, not keeping your methods hidden.
The lesson values reasoning and listening to arguments, not only arguments written as equations.
Checking your calculations a second way is part of what the lesson calls doing math well.
choiceFeedbackEs: La lección trata de compartir y explicar tu razonamiento, no de esconder tus métodos.
La lección valora el razonamiento y escuchar argumentos, no solo los que usan ecuaciones.
Revisar tus cálculos de una segunda manera es parte de lo que la lección llama hacer buenas matemáticas.

turnAndTalk.question: Yuzuki can buy three large boxes (240 cubic inches each) or two jumbo boxes (400 cubic inches each) for the same price. Which option gives more cereal, and how do you know?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Three large boxes hold 240 × 3 = 720 cubic inches, and two jumbo boxes hold 400 × 2 = 800 cubic inches, so 800 > 720.

stems.en: Three large boxes hold ___ cubic inches, and two jumbo boxes hold ___ cubic inches.
stems.es: Tres cajas grandes contienen ___ pulgadas cúbicas, y dos cajas jumbo contienen ___ pulgadas cúbicas.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer calculates both totals (720 and 800) and compares them to recommend the jumbo boxes. A weak answer picks an option without computing and comparing both volumes.
turnAndTalk.extend: Yuzuki's friend argues 'more boxes always means more cereal.' Is she right? Use the numbers to prove your point.
extendStems: The friend is wrong because three boxes give ___ cubic inches, which is ___ than two boxes' ___ cubic inches.
This shows that number of boxes alone does not tell you ___.

turnAndTalk.question: You sorted '800 > 720' as an equation argument and 'the cereal stays fresher' as a word argument. Why are both considered legitimate math arguments, even though only one uses numbers?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The lesson treats both equation-based arguments (like 800 > 720) and word-based arguments (like less packaging) as valid ways to defend a choice.

stems.en: This is an equation argument because it uses ___.
stems.es: Este es un argumento con ecuaciones porque usa ___.

stems.en: This is a word argument because it explains ___ without numbers.
stems.es: Este es un argumento con palabras porque explica ___ sin números.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students explaining that both types of arguments can convince someone, just using different evidence (numbers vs. reasoning). A weak answer dismisses word arguments as 'not real math.'
turnAndTalk.extend: Which single card did you find MOST convincing, and what would make an argument even stronger than that one?
extendStems: The most convincing card was ___ because ___.
An even stronger argument would add ___.

turnAndTalk.question: A community garden design needs 48 cubic feet of soil. Why must the group label their answer in cubic feet instead of just 'feet'?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Volume covers three dimensions, so 48 cubic feet of soil must be labeled in cubic units, not plain feet.

stems.en: The unit must be cubic feet because volume covers ___ dimensions.
stems.es: La unidad debe ser pies cúbicos porque el volumen abarca ___ dimensiones.

stems.en: Finding the volume two different ways and getting matching totals shows the solution is ___.
stems.es: Hallar el volumen de dos maneras diferentes y obtener totales iguales muestra que la solución es ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer explains that volume measures length, width, and height together, so the unit must be cubed. A weak answer says 'because it's soil' without connecting to the three dimensions.
turnAndTalk.extend: If the garden bed were only 24 cubic feet instead of 48, would the group need more or less soil? Justify using the cubic-feet reasoning.
extendStems: With 24 cubic feet, the group would need ___ soil than before because ___.
This still uses cubic feet because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice, one problem asked about calories on a plate with 4 egg muffins at about 60 calories each. What strategy did you use to find about 240?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 4 muffins at about 60 calories each is 60 × 4 = 240 calories, using equal groups.

stems.en: I multiplied ___ by ___ to find the total calories.
stems.es: Multipliqué ___ por ___ para hallar el total de calorías.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students naming the multiplication strategy (4 groups of 60) rather than just stating '240.' A weak answer gives the number with no explanation.
turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who added 60 + 4 instead of multiplying? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ because ___.
Their mistake happens when you ___ instead of ___.

questions.stem: A tram carries 10 passengers each trip. How many trips move 40 passengers?
questions.stemEs: Un tranvía lleva 10 pasajeros en cada viaje. ¿Cuántos viajes se necesitan para mover 40 pasajeros?
choicesEs: 4 viajes
10 viajes
30 viajes
400 viajes
choiceFeedback: That's how many passengers ride each trip, not how many trips are needed in total.
That comes from subtracting the numbers instead of dividing the total by the group size.
That comes from multiplying instead of dividing the total by the group size.
choiceFeedbackEs: Ese es el número de pasajeros por viaje, no cuántos viajes se necesitan en total.
Eso sale de restar los números en vez de dividir el total entre el tamaño del grupo.
Eso sale de multiplicar en vez de dividir el total entre el tamaño del grupo.

questions.explanation: Multiplying by 10 shifts each digit one place left: 2.5 × 10 = 25.
questions.explanationEs: Multiplicar por 10 mueve cada dígito un lugar a la izquierda: 2.5 × 10 = 25.
choiceFeedback: That's the original number — multiplying by 10 should change how big it is.
That comes from dividing by 2, not from multiplying by 10.
That shifts the decimal two places instead of one — multiplying by 10 shifts it only once.
choiceFeedbackEs: Ese es el número original — multiplicar por 10 debería cambiar su tamaño.
Eso sale de dividir entre 2, no de multiplicar por 10.
Eso corre el punto decimal dos lugares en vez de uno — multiplicar por 10 lo corre solo una vez.

questions.stem: Multiplying a whole number by 10 makes the number…
questions.explanation: Multiplying by 10 makes an amount ten times as large — 6 becomes 60.
questions.stemEs: Multiplicar un número entero por 10 hace que el número sea…
choicesEs: 10 más de lo que era
diez veces más pequeño
exactamente igual
diez veces más grande
questions.explanationEs: Multiplicar por 10 hace que una cantidad sea diez veces más grande: 6 se convierte en 60.
choiceFeedback: Multiplying scales the whole number rather than just adding a fixed amount to it.
Multiplying by 10 makes a number grow — dividing by 10 is what would shrink it.
Multiplying by a number other than 1 always changes the size of the number.
choiceFeedbackEs: Multiplicar escala el número completo en vez de solo sumarle una cantidad fija.
Multiplicar por 10 hace crecer un número — dividir entre 10 es lo que lo haría más pequeño.
Multiplicar por un número distinto de 1 siempre cambia el tamaño del número.

items.meaning: A mathematical statement you believe is true but have not yet
A single example that shows a statement is not always true

steps: 1. State a clear claim or conjecture supported by calculations
2. Use accurate units and vocabulary (e.g. cubic units for volume)
3. Test with counterexamples to verify that the rule holds true every time

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Another Option for the Community Garden
revealWordProblem.text:
Another design for the community garden bed, shown here, is also being considered. Both designs are built from rectangular boxes with the same depth.
Question: Which garden bed design would you recommend, and why?
revealWordProblem.imageAlt: Two labeled garden-bed designs built from rectangular boxes, with side lengths marked in feet.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: I broke each design into rectangular boxes, used the labeled lengths to find the area (or volume) of each box, and added the parts to get a total for each design. Then I compared the totals and recommended the design with more planting space for the same depth. I named the numbers I compared so my recommendation is backed by the measurements, not just by how the design looks.
